[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of the 'bitter lesson' versus architectural constraints, e.g., comparing scaling-based models with neuro-symbolic or hybrid systems on tasks requiring compositional generalization and causal inference. — Identifies fundamental limits of pure scaling, such as the inability to learn causal structures from passive text, which would refute the hypothesis if no scaling path overcomes these gaps.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published scaling law studies (e.g., Kaplan et al., Hoffmann et al.) and AGI timelines (e.g., from AI Impacts, Epoch AI), including critiques of scaling as a path to AGI. — Synthesizes existing empirical and theoretical evidence to assess whether the trend supports or contradicts the claim that scaling alone will lead to AGI within 20 years.

C005.subject: Fundamental barriers in reasoning and causal understanding

[PATH:empirical] Systematic evaluation of large language models on out-of-distribution causal reasoning benchmarks (e.g., BERT, GPT-4, Gemini) using tasks from the CausalBench or CLAD dataset, measuring performance degradation relative to in-distribution accuracy. — If scaling alone overcomes fundamental causal reasoning barriers, performance on these benchmarks should improve with model size and data; persistent failure would confirm the hypothesis that inductive biases are missing.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of the sample complexity and generalization bounds for causal discovery in high-dimensional settings, comparing deep learning architectures with explicit causal models (e.g., structural causal models, Bayesian nets). — Proving that current architectures require exponentially more data to learn causal structures than human-like inductive biases would support the existence of fundamental barriers; showing that scaling reduces this gap would refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published results from AGI scaling efforts (e.g., DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic) on tasks requiring intervention-based reasoning, counterfactual inference, and transfer learning, focusing on trends over the past 5 years. — A comprehensive review can reveal whether performance on causal tasks is plateauing or improving with scale, providing evidence for or against the claim that scaling will overcome fundamental reasoning barriers within 20 years.

qualifier.tension: Posits that current deep learning paradigms lack necessary inductive biases for true generalization and causal reasoning, creating friction with the optimistic scaling view.

C008.subject: Embodiment and situated interaction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Embodiment and situated interaction AGI, making a 20-year timeline plausible]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative performance benchmarks of LLM-based agents (e.g., in virtual environments like Minecraft or WebArena) vs. physically embodied robots on tasks requiring real-world interaction (e.g., object manipulation, navigation with obstacles). — If LLM-only agents achieve comparable or superior performance on tasks that supposedly require situated interaction, this would refute the necessity of embodiment. Conversely, a consistent gap favoring embodied systems would support the hypothesis that embodiment is needed, challenging a 20-year timeline.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of causal reasoning and grounding in LLMs vs. embodied systems (e.g., from the 'symbol grounding problem' literature and recent work on sensorimotor contingencies). — A formal argument showing that abstract reasoning can be fully grounded through language alone (e.g., via large-scale linguistic statistics) would weaken the necessity of embodiment. If instead, grounding requires physical interaction, this would strengthen the hypothesis that embodiment is a precondition for AGI.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal studies of AI systems trained purely on text vs. those with embodied experience (e.g., from projects like 'Grounded Language Learning' or 'Robotic Imitation Learning'), focusing on generalization to novel, real-world scenarios. — Evidence that text-only systems fail to generalize to tasks requiring physical commonsense (e.g., predicting object stability or tool use) would confirm the hypothesis. If they succeed, this would refute the claim that embodiment is necessary, making a 20-year timeline more plausible.

qualifier.tension: Highlights that AGI may require physical interaction with the world, a dimension largely absent in current LLM-based approaches, further challenging the scaling-only narrative.

[SYNTHESIS] Both hypotheses agree that embodiment is not necessary for AGI within 20 years, yet the identical wording masks a potential false consensus. The refined claim acknowledges the shared conclusion while introducing nuance: the necessity may vary by AGI architecture, domain, or safety requirements, and the high confidence in the original claims may be overstated due to lack of disconfirming evidence. This reframing turns the apparent contradiction into a productive ambiguity that invites further empirical and theoretical differentiation.

qualifier.tension: Highlights that AGI may require physical interaction with the world, a dimension largely absent in current LLM-based approaches, further challenging the scaling-only narrative.
